title: Satyavati
hook: with the Kuru line about to end, Satyavati asks Bhishma to break his vow, and he refuses her
carry: I will not give up truth

segments.voice: Yesterday: three princesses from Kashi, Amba let go, and a young king dead without a son. She had already chosen.

A family line is a thin thread, and Satyavati has watched hers fray to almost nothing. Her husband is gone. Both of her sons by him are gone. Two young widows grieve in the palace. The only grown man of the house is Bhishma, who swore years ago, so her sons would rule, never to take the throne and never to father children. Now she calls him in. The woman his vow was made for is about to ask him to break it.
screen: `A HUSBAND, TWO SONS, GONE.` → `ONE MAN LEFT.` → `SHE CALLS HIM IN.`

segments.voice: Satyavati makes her case carefully, like someone who has thought about it at night. The offerings to the ancestors, the name of Shantanu, the whole house, she says, now rest on you. You know what dharma asks. Take the throne, and raise children with your brother's widows, so the line goes on. She isn't asking lightly. In the world of the poem, a line with no sons means no one to make the offerings for the dead. But Bhishma says no. He reminds her what he swore, and why: so that her children would rule. Then he says something like this: he could give up the three worlds, the kingdom of the gods, anything greater still, but he will not give up truth. The earth could lose its scent, water its wetness, the sun its glory, before he breaks his word. Hear how strange that is. The vow that made her a queen now stands between her and an heir. Her father's condition drew that vow out once. Now she asks for it back, and it won't come. Some readers see the poem's picture of keeping one's word at any cost. Some see the first sign that his vow will cost his family dearly. The text gives both room. Satyavati asks once more, for the need of the moment, and he still holds. But she has one thing she hasn't told anyone yet.
screen: `THE ANCESTORS' OFFERINGS.` · `TAKE THE THRONE, SHE ASKS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE UP TRUTH.` · `THE VOW THAT MADE HER QUEEN.`

segments.voice: Bhishma's word held, even when the person it served asked him to drop it. Bring to mind one promise you're still keeping, maybe a small one, and hold it without deciding anything. Ask it quietly: who is this still for?
Satyavati. The queen who asks Bhishma to break the vow that made her queen, and hears him refuse.
Your line: I will not give up truth. Tomorrow, Satyavati tells her secret. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu tradition, offerings to the ancestors are called shraddha, and some families keep the season called Pitru Paksha for them; the worry in this story is that no one will be left to make them.

fork.setup: you're Bhishma. the queen your vow was made for asks you to break it. what do you do?
options: break it, for the family's sake.
fork.reveal: he refuses: the earth could lose its scent before he gave up his word.

original.note: Sanskrit satya: truth, the thing Bhishma says he will never give up.

trapdoor: what you thought: a stubborn man saying no.
what it means: a vow made for Satyavati now blocking what she needs.
what a scholar hears: Bhishma's refusal lists what nature might give up before he would give up truth.

chat.says: Why wouldn't Bhishma take the throne, even when Satyavati herself asked him?
options: He'd sworn an oath, and he said he would not give up truth, whatever it cost.
He thought Vichitravirya's widows should rule Hastinapura together.
He was waiting for the learned men of the court to approve it first.
chat.meaning: Bhishma had sworn never to take the throne or father children. He told her he would not give up truth.

Shantanu.meaning: the Kuru king, Satyavati's husband and Bhishma's father

Bhishma.meaning: Shantanu's son, who vowed never to take the throne

Satyavati.meaning: the fisherman's daughter who became queen mother of the Kurus

recall: Ganga's son, a name for Bhishma
whose request ended the snake sacrifice

notes: All paraphrase, including Bhishma's speech (the three worlds; earth giving up its scent, water its moisture, the sun its light). Confirm the list in Ganguli; it was not quoted because the exact wording was not certain.
